newsitem.title: USA: Miami Heat says no to arena site switch.
newsitem.headline: Miami Heat says no to arena site switch.

text.p: The Miami Heat said Tuesday it could not accept any site for its new arena other than the waterfront park land specified in a referendum that voters approved last fall.
"We took a position on that, that that would be unacceptable," Heat Vice President Steve Watson said.

The announcement came a day after Dade County Mayor Alex Penelas asked County Manager Armando Vidal to scout out other potential sites because the county was unable to reach a lease agreement with the City of Miami, which owns the waterfront site.
The Heat have agreed to pay for the $228 million arena, using privately placed bonds via Prudential Securities Inc. The bonds would be repaid with revenues from the 20,000-seat facility.
Under its agreement with the team, Dade County would own the arena and would contribute $6.5 million of bed tax revenues annually for 30 years to pay operating costs.
Voters agreed last fall to let the Heat build the arena on the public park land as part of a 59-acre project that will include retail space, public parks and an extension of the Port of Miami.

The county, which owns the seaport, has been unable to come to terms with the city. The county had tentatively agreed to pay $97 million for a 45-year lease for the property, but the deal unraveled Monday after the city added lease terms the county found unacceptable.
Those included a requirement that the county build and pay for a $2 million fire station on the land and that the county pay off $3.95 million of city park bonds used to aquire the property.
The Heat called a news conference to announce its position Monday, hoping to pressure the city to come to terms quickly.
"If you start eviscerating that project, you compromise the entire development," Watson told Reuters.

"We're on a serious time frame, which I think people also need to be aware of. To make this arena affordable, we need to begin construction this fall in order to move in by the start of the 1999 season," Watson.
He said the team's statement should not be viewed as an ultimatum or a threat to leave town.
"We're not about packing up our toys and going home," he said.
